title: Title And Problem: Supersampling Half-Plane Discrepancy
notes: Begin from the rendering motivation on printed pages 173-174: ray tracing estimates what fraction of a pixel is covered by a surface, and supersampling replaces a continuous area question by finitely many sample probes. The lecture problem is to place samples so every local edge half-plane is counted nearly in proportion to its area.

title: Why Half-Planes: Pixel Edge As Local Half-Plane
notes: Use the pixel-edge picture to justify the abstraction rather than assuming it. At the scale of one pixel, a smooth boundary is approximated by a line, so the visible part of the pixel is one side of that line. The source discussion on printed pages 173-174 motivates why half-planes are the stress test for sample patterns.

title: Continuous vs Discrete Measure: Area Versus Sample Count
notes: Now formalize the mismatch from printed pages 175-177. The continuous quantity is area fraction inside a region, while the discrete estimator is the fraction of stored samples in the same region. Discrepancy measures the worst absolute gap over all half-planes; low discrepancy means the sample set behaves like area for every edge position.

title: Infinite Search Becomes Candidates
notes: Printed pages 175-177 show the first finiteness move. Although there are infinitely many half-planes, the sample count changes only when the boundary crosses a sample point. Between such events, the area changes continuously while the count is fixed, so maxima can be hunted among boundaries touching points and among extreme placements.

title: Theorem 8.2 Route Map: Type-I, Dualize Type-II, Arrangement Levels
notes: Present Theorem 8.2 as a route map, not as a copied proof. The chapter separates candidate half-planes into direct type-I cases and type-II cases that become easier after duality. The arrangement of dual lines then organizes the relevant level counts, tying the discrepancy computation to planar subdivision machinery.

title: Point-Line Duality Definition: (a,b) To y=ax-b
notes: Introduce the duality from printed pages 177-179 with the exact mapping used in the chapter. A primal point (a,b) becomes the nonvertical line y equals ax minus b. A primal nonvertical line y equals mx plus c becomes the dual point (m,-c). The sign convention is chosen so incidence and vertical order line up cleanly.

title: Incidence And Order Preservation
notes: Stay on printed pages 177-179 and emphasize what the transformation buys us. If a primal point lies on a primal line, the dual line passes through the dual point. If the primal point is above the primal line, then at the dual x-coordinate the dual line is below the dual point, giving a controlled reversal that still preserves order information.

title: Vertical Lines And Segment Wedges
notes: Handle the caveat that ordinary point-line duality avoids vertical primal lines. For a vertical segment or a pair of points with the same x-coordinate, the set of compatible nonvertical lines appears as a wedge or interval of slopes in the dual plane. This is the geometric bridge needed before counting candidates from point pairs.

title: Discrepancy In The Dual Plane: Primal Pair Line To Dual Vertex Counts
notes: Move from duality to discrepancy. A primal line through two samples corresponds to the intersection vertex of their two dual lines. Counting how many primal points lie on one side becomes counting how many dual lines lie above or below that vertex. This is where the half-plane discrepancy problem becomes a level query in an arrangement.

title: Arrangement Complexity: Simple vs Degenerate Arrangements
notes: Use printed pages 179-182 to define arrangements as the subdivision induced by lines. In simple position, every pair meets once and no three lines meet at one point, giving a clean quadratic count of vertices, edges, and faces. Degeneracies collapse events and require consistent handling, but the subdivision viewpoint remains the same.

title: Why A Bounding Box And DCEL
notes: The arrangement is easier to store when it is clipped to a large box, because every face boundary becomes finite. The DCEL records directed half-edges with twin, next, previous, incident face, and origin links. Printed pages 179-182 use this structure so local edits can update topology without rebuilding the whole subdivision.

title: Incremental Construction Walk
notes: Explain the incremental construction from printed pages 179-182. Insert lines one by one. For the new line, find its intersections with the existing subdivision in order, walk through the sequence of crossed faces, and split those faces as the line segment inside the bounding box is added.

title: Face Split Operation
notes: Zoom in on the DCEL operation behind the previous slide. When a new line cuts through a face, two new half-edges separate the old boundary cycle into two face cycles. The important teaching point is local topology: only pointers around the crossed face and the new edge pieces change.

title: Zone Theorem As The Runtime Lens
notes: Printed pages 183-185 introduce the zone theorem as the lens for runtime. The zone of a line is the collection of arrangement faces the line crosses. Even though the whole arrangement may be quadratic, the total complexity of this crossed strip is linear in the number of existing lines, so one insertion can be charged locally.

title: Level Walk Along A Line
notes: Use printed pages 185-186 to connect arrangements to levels. The k-level consists of points that have exactly k lines strictly below them. Walking along a line from left to right, the level changes by one at every crossing, so the arrangement supplies the sequence of counts needed for discrepancy.

title: Discrepancy From Levels And Takeaways
notes: Close by summarizing the pipeline from printed pages 186-190. Supersampling asks for area versus count agreement over all half-planes. Candidate reduction makes the search finite, duality converts side counts into line levels, and arrangements with DCEL and zone analysis make those levels algorithmically accessible.
